filename: A Case Study on the Acceptance of a Humanoid Robotic Head.pdf
summary:
This study examines how visitors across three public locations in Stuttgart, Germany received Kim, a humanoid android robot head. Researchers deployed Kim at a tourist information center, a building authority, and a city library between May and June 2025, gathering responses from 49 participants total.

Kim's technical stack combines Whisper for speech recognition, XTTS for text-to-speech, FaceXHubert for lip-sync, and ChatGPT 4.1 with location-specific RAG knowledge bases for responses. Emotional expressions are driven by the WASABI affect simulation system.

Acceptance was measured using TAM2, evaluating Intention to Use (ITU), Perceived Usefulness (PU), and Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU). All median scores exceeded 4 on a 7-point scale across every location. Kruskal-Wallis tests revealed no statistically significant differences between sites for any construct, suggesting the deployment environment did not meaningfully affect user acceptance. Participants interacted in 17 languages, with German, English, and French being most common. Average interaction time was around 7 minutes.

Descriptively, the building authority showed lower ITU and usefulness ratings, aligning with prior research suggesting robots face greater resistance in administrative contexts. Key limitations include the small sample — particularly at the building authority — and uncontrolled interaction dynamics inherent to open public settings. The authors recommend future comparisons with less anthropomorphic robots and more controlled experimental designs to build on these findings.

filename: A Taxonomy of Cognitive Capability Gaps in Generative and Agentic AI.pdf
summary:
This paper addresses the problem of cognitive capability gaps in contemporary generative and agentic AI systems, arguing that strong benchmark performance should not be conflated with cognition and that fundamental cognitive functions remain fragmented or absent, limiting reliable long-term autonomous operation.

The methodology is a narrative synthesis of literature spanning cognitive architectures, foundation models, agentic AI, memory systems, reasoning, metacognition, environment interaction, world modeling, and continual learning. The authors propose a taxonomy organizing gaps into five dimensions: Persistent State Modeling (persistent memory, state revision, latent state modeling), Goal-Directed Autonomy (goal formulation, planning and adaptation, goal persistence), Self-Monitoring and Control (metacognitive monitoring, uncertainty and OOD detection, abstention and control), Environment Interaction (world modeling, tool-augmented reasoning, environment feedback loops), and Learning and Adaptation (policy adaptation, continual learning, safe knowledge updates).

Key named concepts include Cognitive AI, meaning systems capable of sustained reasoning, persistent memory, and self-regulation, distinct from generative AI and agentic AI. ACIA (Adaptive Cognitive Intelligence Architecture) is the closed-loop architecture proposed by the authors, with six components: Perception and Attention, Memory (working, episodic, semantic), Reasoning and Planning, Metacognition, Action, and Learning and Adaptation. Goal drift is gradual deviation from intended objectives across interactions. Catastrophic forgetting is degradation of prior knowledge when learning new tasks. The alignment tax is the reduction in general reasoning capability from domain-specific fine-tuning. Three cognition-centric evaluation metrics are proposed: Cognitive Persistence Index (CPI), measuring retention and retrieval accuracy across extended interactions; Cognitive Adaptation Rate (CAR), measuring successful adaptation while preserving prior knowledge; and Cognitive Consistency Score (CCS), measuring coherence of beliefs and reasoning over time as a function of contradictions relative to total reasoning episodes. Representative systems cited include MemGPT, AriGraph, Reflexion, Chain-of-Thought, ROME, MEMIT, EWC, and the Belief-R benchmark.

The paper reports no original empirical results, as it is a survey. The Belief-R benchmark is cited to illustrate that many models struggle to reliably update conclusions when presented with new information.

The authors conclude that achieving Cognitive AI requires advances beyond parameter scaling, specifically persistent internal state, autonomous metacognitive control, continual learning without forgetting, and safe knowledge updating. They call for longitudinal evaluation frameworks assessing memory retention, goal stability, and reasoning consistency across extended interactions, and note that increasing autonomy demands greater attention to safety, transparency, and human oversight.

CATTLE TRADE is a multi-agent benchmark for evaluating large language models as strategic agents under imperfect information, adversarial interaction, and resource constraints. It addresses a gap in existing LLM evaluation: prior benchmarks test strategic skills such as deception, negotiation, or game-theoretic reasoning in isolation, but none require agents to combine auctions, hidden-offer bargaining, bluffing, and resource management within a single long-horizon competitive game.

The benchmark adapts Kuhhandel, a tabletop card game by Rudiger Koltze (Ravensburger, 1985). Players collect quartets — complete sets of 4 cards of one animal type — across 10 animal types scored multiplicatively: final score equals completed quartet values times the number of completed quartets, ranging from Chicken (10) to Horse (1000). Money cards use fixed denominations (0 to 500) with no change given; each player starts with 90 coins, over 50-60 turns with 4 players. Two mechanics drive strategy: auctions with a buy-right option (the auctioneer may pay the winning bid to keep the card instead of selling), and hidden-offer trade challenges (TCs), where a player makes a face-down offer for a shared animal type and the opponent accepts blind or counters, the higher offer winning. Zero-denomination cards enable bluffing since opponents can't distinguish a genuine offer from a worthless one.

Seven cost-efficient LLMs were evaluated: Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite (G2.5-FL), Gemini 3 Flash Preview (G3-F), Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite Preview (G3.1-FL), GPT-5.4 Nano (GPT5.4-N), and DeepSeek v3.2 (DS-v3.2), plus three code-agent baselines: TrackerAgent (tracks cards, bids on inferred opponent wealth), SetRaceAgent (greedy quartet completion), and EconomyAgent (caps spending per turn). 242 games ran across 60 pure-LLM and 168 mixed-format matches. Agents were rated via TrueSkill, a Bayesian skill-rating system yielding a mean mu and standard deviation sigma.

Key metrics: capital efficiency (eta) is score divided by coin outflow, exceeding 1.0 when free acquisitions and won bluffs amplify returns; TC bargaining tightness (tau) is the ratio of loser offer to winner offer across counter-wins, near 1 for minimal necessary overpay and near 0 for a crushing overpay; bid aggressiveness is mean bid-to-quartet-value ratio; self-bid percentage is bids with no competing bid since the agent's last; overbid percentage is auctions bid beyond total money; buy-right percentage is auctioneer turns keeping the card; bluff percentage is TC offers made entirely of 0-value cards.

Across 98 canonical games, TrueSkill rankings placed G3-F first (mu 30.1, 72.9% win rate, median score 5,250), TrackerAgent second (28.7, 53.6% wins), G3.1-FL third (28.0, 44.9% wins), SetRaceAgent fourth (27.3), Sonnet 4.5 fifth (26.4, 35.7% wins), then DS-v3.2 (23.9), GPT5.4-N (22.6), EconomyAgent (22.1), Haiku (21.8), and G2.5-FL last (20.5, 0.0% wins) — TrackerAgent beat six of seven LLMs, SetRaceAgent five. Capital efficiency for top agents was eta 1.77 (G3-F), 1.55 (TrackerAgent), 1.46 (G3.1-FL), while G2.5-FL reached only 0.23 despite the highest bid aggressiveness (2.52), paying a median 1,193 coins per quartet versus 600-750 for top agents. G3-F escalated aggressiveness from 0.26 early-game to 2.49 late; G2.5-FL stayed flat near 2.07. DS-v3.2 and G2.5-FL self-bid over 74% of rounds, G3.1-FL under 7%. Token usage varied 20-fold (~275,000 completion tokens per game for G3-F versus 14,800 for G3.1-FL), yet both ranked top-tier, indicating verbose reasoning isn't required for strong play.

The authors conclude strategic coherence — spending efficiency, resource discipline, phase-adaptive bidding — predicts rank more strongly than any single subskill. Failure modes such as overbidding, self-bidding spirals, and bankrupt TC initiation are invisible to static benchmarks but directly observable in CATTLE TRADE's structured game logs. Future directions include evaluating frontier models at full reasoning budgets, enabling inter-agent communication, self-play fine-tuning to eliminate specific failure modes, and benchmarking against human players.

This paper addresses the challenge of predicting financial distress in enterprises when bankrupt firms represent a small minority of observations in real-world datasets, causing conventional classifiers to achieve high aggregate accuracy while failing to detect distress events with adequate sensitivity. The operational motivation is that false negatives delay intervention and increase financial exposure.

The study uses the Taiwan Economic Journal corporate bankruptcy dataset comprising approximately 6,819 firm-level observations across 96 financial features, with bankrupt firms constituting roughly 1.8 percent of total observations. The methodology follows a CRISP-DM-oriented workflow covering median imputation, StandardScaler normalisation, correlation-based feature filtering, an 80/20 train-test split, and SMOTE applied exclusively to the training partition. Six models were compared: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost, CatBoost, and LightGBM, with exploratory LSTM, ARIMA, and SARIMA approaches also assessed. SHAP explainability analysis was applied to best-performing models. All experiments used scikit-learn, XGBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM, PyTorch, and SHAP.

Key terms: SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique) generates synthetic minority-class samples via nearest-neighbour interpolation to balance class distribution during training. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) estimates each feature's marginal contribution to model output using cooperative game-theoretic principles. CRISP-DM (Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining) is the structured workflow framework governing the pipeline. ROC-AUC measures discriminatory capability across classification thresholds. Recall, treated as the primary metric due to the asymmetric cost of false negatives, measures the proportion of actual bankruptcies detected. Precision measures the proportion of predicted bankruptcies that are correct. F1-score is their harmonic mean.

Quantitative results: Logistic Regression achieved precision 0.41, recall 0.52, F1 0.46, ROC-AUC 0.71. Random Forest: 0.63, 0.74, 0.68, 0.84. AdaBoost: 0.59, 0.69, 0.63, 0.81. XGBoost: 0.71, 0.83, 0.76, 0.91. CatBoost: 0.69, 0.81, 0.74, 0.89. LightGBM: 0.67, 0.79, 0.72, 0.88. XGBoost's confusion matrix showed 1,312 true negatives, 48 false positives, 19 false negatives, and 85 true positives. SHAP analysis identified debt ratio, retained earnings, liquidity ratio, operating margin, and total assets as the top predictive features.

The authors conclude that gradient-boosting ensembles, particularly XGBoost, provide the strongest minority-class recall and discriminatory performance under severe imbalance, substantially outperforming logistic regression. SMOTE improved minority-class sensitivity but introduced moderate precision-recall trade-offs. Future work suggested includes deeper investigation of LSTM, ARIMA, and SARIMA temporal approaches, more advanced imbalance mitigation strategies, and governance-oriented orchestration frameworks for production deployment.

filename: Deep Learning Approaches for Early Detection of Chronic Diseases-A Comprehensive Review.pdf
summary:
This review paper, authored by Kummaragunta Joel Prabhod (Senior Machine Learning Engineer, Thought Green Technologies), published in Distributed Learning and Broad Applications in Scientific Research, synthesizes literature and clinical trials up to March 2021 on deep learning approaches for early detection of three chronic disease categories: diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer. It is a literature synthesis rather than original experimental research, examining architectures and their reported clinical applications across medical imaging, electronic health records, and genomic data.

Three architecture families are covered. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) process spatial data such as medical images through convolutional layers (learnable filters detecting local patterns like edges and textures), pooling layers (which downsample feature maps and reduce dimensionality), and fully connected layers that produce final classifications; named CNN variants discussed include ResNet, DenseNet, VGGNet, and Inception. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) handle sequential and time-series data by propagating a hidden state across time steps, but suffer vanishing/exploding gradient problems on long sequences; this is addressed by Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, which use memory cells and gating mechanisms to retain long-term dependencies, and by Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), a simplified LSTM variant. Hybrid models combine CNNs for spatial feature extraction with RNNs for temporal dependencies, used for data with both dimensions, such as imaging sequences paired with time-series patient monitoring.

Model performance is evaluated using several named metrics: sensitivity (also called recall) is the proportion of true positives correctly identified, TP/(TP+FN); specificity is the proportion of true negatives correctly identified, TN/(TN+FP); precision is the proportion of positive predictions that are correct, TP/(TP+FP); the F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, used especially for imbalanced datasets; and AUC-ROC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve) measures a model's ability to discriminate between classes across thresholds, ranging from 0.5 (random guessing) to 1.0 (perfect), with values above 0.8 generally considered good. Cross-validation techniques discussed include k-fold, leave-one-out (LOOCV), and stratified cross-validation, which preserves class distribution across folds.

For diabetes, the review cites a Google Health study using CNNs on retinal fundus images to detect diabetic retinopathy at accuracy comparable to human ophthalmologists, an LSTM-based glucose-prediction study published in the Journal of Diabetes Science and Technology, and a UCSF hybrid CNN-LSTM model combining retinal imaging with continuous glucose monitoring. For cardiovascular disease, it cites a University of Oxford CNN detecting myocardial infarction from cardiac MRI, an LSTM-based arrhythmia detection model (Circulation: Arrhythmia and Electrophysiology) identifying atrial fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia from ECG recordings, and a Cleveland Clinic hybrid model combining cardiac CT with wearable ECG data. For cancer, it covers a Google Health mammography CNN for breast cancer exceeding radiologist-level performance, a National Cancer Institute 3D CNN with radiomic features for lung nodule detection, a UCLA CNN for prostate cancer segmentation on multi-parametric MRI, and a Stanford dermoscopic-image CNN for skin cancer classification matching dermatologist accuracy.

Recurring limitations across all three disease areas: data privacy and security requirements (HIPAA, GDPR, anonymization risk); the need for large, expert-annotated datasets, which are costly and slow to produce; model interpretability, since deep learning models function as "black boxes" — addressed through explainable AI (XAI) techniques including saliency maps, Grad-CAM, SHAP, and LIME, which attribute predictions to specific input features; and generalization across diverse patient populations, where non-representative training data produces biased results. The review concludes that deep learning shows substantial diagnostic promise across all three disease categories, but that clinical adoption depends on resolving these interpretability, privacy, and generalization challenges, pointing to multi-modal learning, self-supervised learning, federated learning, and transformer-based architectures as the main directions for future work.

filename: Deep Learning Techniques for the Effective Prediction of.pdf
summary:
This paper addresses the problem of accurately diagnosing and predicting Alzheimer's disease (AD) using deep learning (DL) techniques, motivated by the limitations of traditional machine learning (ML) approaches when handling large-scale, heterogeneous neuroimaging data. The authors provide a comprehensive review of DL architectures applied to AD classification and prognosis, survey real-world case studies, and identify open research challenges in the field.

The methodology is a structured literature review covering studies that applied DL to AD detection using neuroimaging datasets, primarily ADNI (Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative), OASIS (providing MRI and PET data for 1098 subjects), MIRIAD, and AddNeuroMed. The review spans unimodal and multimodal approaches across MRI, FDG-PET, and amyloid PET imaging modalities, and examines both hybrid ML-DL pipelines and end-to-end DL systems.

Key terms: AD (Alzheimer's disease) is the most common form of dementia, involving memory loss and neuronal death across seven clinical phases; MCI (Mild Cognitive Impairment) is its prodromal phase, and CN/NC is the cognitively normal control group. DL (deep learning) is a subset of ML using multi-layered neural networks that learn features directly from raw data. CNN (Convolutional Neural Network) is the most-used discriminative architecture for image feature extraction; RNN (Recurrent Neural Network) handles sequential data and spans both generative and discriminative categories. DAE (Deep Auto-Encoder), DBM (Deep Boltzmann Machine, built from RBMs), and DBN (Deep Belief Network) are unsupervised/supervised generative architectures; RBM (Restricted Boltzmann Machine) reduces hyperparameter sensitivity via weight initialization. AE (Auto-Encoder) uses back-propagation and SGD for dimensionality reduction; SAE (Stacked Sparse Auto-Encoder) restricts active hidden units to address vanishing gradients. ReLu is the standard activation function replacing sigmoid; SGD and Adam are the gradient-descent optimizers used throughout. GAN (Generative Adversarial Network) is proposed for synthetic image augmentation. FDG-PET measures cerebral glucose metabolism. VoxCNN (derived from VGGNet) and VoxResNet are 3D imaging architectures; CapsNets (3D Capsule Networks) enable rapid volumetric scanning. FreeSurfer and SPM5 are standard pre-processing tools; CADe identifies regions of interest and CADx performs diagnostic classification. Transfer learning means fine-tuning pre-trained CNNs such as InceptionV3 or ResNet50 on domain-specific data.

Concrete results across reviewed studies include: SAE with softmax regression achieved over 86% AD/CN accuracy; multimodal SAE with zero-mask fusion achieved over 90%; SAE with DNN achieved over 84% AD/CN and over 82% MCI-to-AD conversion accuracy; 3D-CNN on MRI achieved over 87%, rising to over 89% when combining MRI and PET streams; VoxCNN and ResNet achieved over 79%; 2D CNN on hippocampal slices achieved over 85%; landmark-based 3D CNN achieved over 91% AD/CN and over 75% MCI-to-AD on ADNI-2; combined SAE and 3D CNN achieved 90%; ensemble of 2D CNN and RNN on FDG-PET achieved 91%; 3D CNN on heterogeneous PET achieved over 95% AD/CN and over 84% MCI-to-AD accuracy; 3D CapsNets achieved 98.42% AD identification accuracy; InceptionV3 on FDG-PET achieved 92% and reportedly outperformed clinicians in predicting AD progression more than six years in advance. SVM-based ML baselines achieved 90.5% AD vs. NC accuracy and 72.3% MCI-to-AD prediction accuracy for comparison.

The authors conclude that DL, particularly CNN-based and multimodal approaches, substantially outperforms traditional ML for AD diagnosis and MCI-to-AD conversion prediction, with multimodal neuroimaging consistently exceeding unimodal results. Remaining challenges include data scarcity and class imbalance, overfitting risk, lack of transparency and reproducibility due to the black box nature of DL models, difficulty replicating results across research groups, and ethical constraints around health data access. Future work proposed includes expanding 3D CNN architectures, using GANs for data augmentation, incorporating reinforcement learning for adaptive clinical decisions, and progressing toward purely DL-based pipelines as neuroimaging data volumes and computational resources increase.

This paper addresses the problem of identifying objective speech biomarkers for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), specifically through the dynamical properties of speech articulators, an angle not previously investigated in depression research.

The methodology involves three stages applied to the Androids Corpus, a publicly available dataset of 228 recordings from 118 speakers, including 64 clinically diagnosed with depression by professional psychiatrists and 54 matched controls. Speakers completed a Reading Task and an Interview Task (spontaneous speech). A Speech Inversion step converts audio into six Tract Variables (TVs) using a five-layer feedforward neural network trained on the X-Ray Micro-Beam dataset (XRMB). The six TVs are Lip Aperture (LA), Lip Protrusion (LP), Tongue Body Constriction Location (TBCL), Tongue Body Constriction Degree (TBCD), Tongue Tip Constriction Location (TTCL), and Tongue Tip Constriction Degree (TTCD), each measuring a geometric property of the speech articulators. State-space embeddings are then constructed via Takens' Theorem using the NeuroKit2 package, and three dynamical biomarkers are computed: the Largest Lyapunov Exponent (LLE), measuring articulatory unpredictability; the Correlation Dimension (CD), measuring complexity or degrees of freedom in articulation; and Sample Entropy (SE), measuring the rate of new pattern generation, where lower SE indicates more repetitive sequences. Effect sizes are reported using Cliff's delta, where a value of 0.5 indicates 75 percent of pairwise comparisons favor one group.

Results show depressed speakers have higher LLE (less predictable), lower CD (more constrained), and lower SE (more repetitive) than controls. For the Reading Task, tongue TVs combined yield a Cliff's delta of 0.51 for LLE and all TVs combined yield 0.50. CD differences are significant across all TVs in both tasks, reaching delta 0.49 for all TVs in the Reading Task. SE reaches delta 0.42 for the lips group in the Reading Task. LLE is effective mainly for read speech; CD and SE are effective for both tasks. An SVM classifier using all 18 features achieves 73.2 percent accuracy on the Reading Task, outperforming the Low Level Descriptors baseline at 69.6 percent, with comparable performance on the Interview Task.

The authors conclude that TV dynamics capture depression-relevant articulatory changes across predictability, complexity, and repetitiveness, and that TVs are most discriminative when considered jointly rather than individually. Future work is proposed integrating these biomarkers with foundation models for automated depression detection.

This position and roadmap paper, authored by Nicole Mitchell, Dhruv Agarwal, Maty Bohacek, Remi Denton, and Roma Patel (Google DeepMind, Google Research, Cornell University, Stanford University), argues that NLP safety research must pivot from static, single-session evaluations of language model outputs to longitudinal measurements of human behavioral change resulting from sustained AI interaction. The core claim is that many risks only surface or accumulate across long time horizons and are invisible within any individual session.

The paper is not an empirical study but a synthesis and proposal. It draws on cognitive science, psychology, HCI, and NLP to define a three-part infrastructure: metrics for measuring human behavioral shifts, longitudinal datasets of human-AI interactions, and alignment frameworks targeting long-term user outcomes rather than immediate preferences.

Key terms defined in the paper: synchronic interaction is a single bounded session evaluated at one point in time; diachronic interaction refers to patterns observed across sessions over weeks or months. Longitudinal effects are impacts that only emerge or intensify over extended interaction horizons. Cognitive deskilling is the erosion of a user's own cognitive abilities through habitual AI offloading. Delusional reinforcement (also called AI psychosis) is a sycophantic feedback loop that entrenches distorted beliefs, with risk escalating through accumulated context. Distributed persuasion describes subtle influence spread thinly across sessions to evade single-session detectors. Ideological convergence is population-level alignment of beliefs caused by sustained AI exposure. Value and goal drift refers to shifts in higher-level user preferences over developmental time. Psychometric bias refers to construct and content validity failures when psychological scales are applied to text outside their validation contexts.

The paper taxonomizes longitudinal risks into four categories: socio-affective (parasocial attachment, affective dependence), cognitive (deskilling, miscalibrated trust), epistemic (delusional reinforcement, ideological convergence, distributed persuasion, value drift), and clinical (mental health deterioration, compulsive use). Three data-gathering frameworks are compared: randomized controlled trials (RCTs) allow causal isolation but suffer attrition and observer effects; field studies offer ecological validity but lack causal inference and are constrained by private data ownership; user simulations are scalable but prone to trajectory drift and cannot surface novel risks.

The authors conclude that existing alignment techniques including RLHF and DPO optimize only for immediate preferences and must be extended with longitudinal reward signals, psychometric features as RL feedback, and adaptive safety guardrails triggered at behavioral inflection points. Limitations include corporate data scarcity, western bias in psychometric instruments, and privacy risks requiring federated logging and dynamic consent.

filename: Measuring the Effect of Within-Conversation Context on AI Answers.pdf
summary:
This paper asks whether omitting prior conversational turns materially changes an AI system's answer when the final user message is held constant. AI evaluations commonly treat the final message as the complete query, but in multi-turn conversations, goals and constraints are often distributed across earlier turns and not restated at the end.

The study uses a paired design across 180 English multi-turn conversations drawn equally from a governed commercial corpus and the public PRISM dataset. For each conversation, three answers are generated holding the final message constant: YF from the full role-labelled prefix plus final message, YI from the final message alone, and YC from a compressed prefix reconstruction capped at 160 words plus the final message. The answer model is gpt-5.4-mini and the judge model is gpt-5.5. The primary endpoint is a binary material-difference judgment excluding wording, tone, or detail differences alone. Estimates are inverse-probability-weighted to restore pooled eligible-cohort composition.

The primary weighted estimate finds YF and YI differ materially in 44.7% of cases (95% CI 33.8% to 56.1%), with full-conversation answers scoring 0.49 satisfaction points higher on a 0 to 4 scale. Adding the compressed prefix reduces the material-difference rate to 30.8% and closes the average satisfaction gap to 0.01 points, but nearly one third of answers remain materially different. The material-change rate is 68.5% in the commercial cohort versus 35.4% in PRISM.

The authors conclude that the full conversation, not the final message string, is the defensible query unit for evaluating conversational AI systems.

filename: Understanding Down Syndrome Stereotypes in LLM-Based Personas.pdf
summary:
This paper investigates how stereotypes manifest in large language model (LLM)-based personas representing individuals with Down syndrome, using a system called Persona-L as the case study. The core problem is that existing persona generation approaches, whether data-driven or LLM-based, risk reinforcing oversimplified, stereotypical, or deficit-based portrayals of marginalized populations, and the extent to which interface design and LLM delivery introduce these harms had not been studied.

Persona-L is a web-based interface using LLMs and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to create interactive personas of people with Down syndrome. RAG grounds LLM responses in a curated external knowledge base to reduce hallucination. The system is built on an ability-based framework, foregrounding functional strengths over deficits. The study extended Persona-L by integrating a Stereotype Detection Module built on a curated version of the Multi-Grain Stereotype Dataset (MGSD), originally derived from the StereoSet and CrowS-Pairs datasets with over 51,000 labeled examples. The MGSD was simplified to three labels for this work: stereotype gender, stereotype profession, and neutral, then extended with Down syndrome-specific instances. Thirty seed sentences were manually labeled by three annotators, achieving a Fleiss' Kappa score of 0.775, indicating substantial inter-annotator agreement. GPT-4 expanded these into 500 additional synthetic instances. The final dataset included 16,139 training and 1,769 testing instances across four categories: neutral (896), stereotype profession (647), stereotype gender (218), and stereotype downsyndrome (34). Four transformer-based models were fine-tuned: ELECTRA, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, and DistilBERT. DistilBERT was excluded from the final system due to low accuracy (68%). The remaining three formed an ensemble using majority voting with probability-weighted adjustments, achieving accuracy of 82.06%, precision of 82.74%, recall of 82.06%, and F1-score of 82.16%. Down syndrome stereotype detection specifically achieved an F1-score of 99%. Gender stereotype recall was moderate at 76%. A comparative experiment using paired-sample t-tests across 864 persona response pairs found GPT-4o produced a higher mean Average Stereotype Probability (34.92) than Persona-L (33.64), with t(863) = 4.65, p less than 0.001, indicating RAG reduces stereotype levels in generated output. Average Stereotype Probability is a custom metric computed as the mean confidence-weighted stereotype score across all sentences in a response, where stereotyped sentences contribute their model confidence score directly and neutral sentences contribute 1 minus that score. Flagged sentences were surfaced in the interface with GPT-4-generated natural language explanations and confidence scores as tooltips, without automatic correction, preserving user control.

Qualitative validation involved semi-structured interviews with ten caregivers and specialists (N=10), including parents, siblings, special education teachers, speech-language pathologists, and occupational therapists, each with at least one year of direct experience supporting individuals with Down syndrome. Participants created personas, completed a six-item Likert survey on persona accuracy and trustworthiness, and reviewed system-flagged outputs.

Findings showed stereotypes emerge not only in LLM content but also through interface design, such as capping persona age at 40 (reinforcing outdated life-expectancy assumptions) and occupational categories that were either too aspirational or too narrow, and through delivery style — overly cheerful tone, excessive length, scripted structure, and vocabulary inconsistent with the persona's developmental profile. Caregivers identified the perpetually positive, one-dimensional portrayal as a core stereotype, alongside ableist devaluation, appearance-based assumptions, infantilization, and intellectual inferiority as the most prevalent stereotypes.

The authors conclude that stereotype mitigation requires combining technical detection with participatory design, specifically including caregivers and individuals with Down syndrome as co-designers at all stages. Future work suggested includes crowdsourcing lived experience data directly from the Down syndrome community, tuning Persona-L to match authentic communication rhythms and brevity, and offering layered persona views representing both the individual with Down syndrome and caregiver or therapist perspectives to balance authenticity with accessibility for design teams.
